subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Write the equation for the carbylamine reaction of any one aliphatic amine.

mark_split.label: Conditions and what the test shows

verification.note: Unit 18 (Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.115-120, from the shaded sub-box "ORGANIC COMPOUNDS CONTAINING NITROGEN" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.115 as VSAQ 6. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. EQUATION CHECKED: CH₃NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → CH₃NC + 3KCl + 3H₂O balances on every element — C 2/2, H 9/9, N 1/1, Cl 3/3, K 3/3, O 3/3. The book prints the same equation and it is correct. BOOK GAP (book p.115, VSAQ 6): the printed answer says only that primary amines give isocyanides and that the reaction is used to detect them. It never says that 2° and 3° amines give NO isocyanide, which is what makes this a test at all; that is added here. The book also writes "alcoholic KOH" in the words and bare "3KOH" in the equation — the reagent is alcoholic KOH and the card says so.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The balanced equation
lines: Methanamine is used as the aliphatic amine.
The product CH₃–NC is methyl isocyanide,
steps.why: Chloroform and alkali give dichlorocarbene, and the amine nitrogen bonds to its carbon. Both hydrogen atoms of the –NH₂ group and all three chlorine atoms of chloroform are removed, which is why three formula units of KOH are needed and three of KCl and water are produced.
common_mistakes: Writing KOH without a coefficient. Three KOH are needed to remove three chlorine atoms, so the equation does not balance with one.
Writing the product as CH₃–CN. That is methyl cyanide; the carbylamine product is the isocyanide CH₃–NC, joined through nitrogen.
steps.memory_tip: One amine, one chloroform, three KOH, and three each of KCl and water come out.
steps.margin_note: Balance the equation before writing it down. An unbalanced carbylamine equation loses this mark even if the products are right.

steps.label: Conditions and the test
lines: The amine is warmed with chloroform and
The isocyanide formed has a strong
unpleasant smell, which is how it is noticed.
2° and 3° amines give no isocyanide at all,
so the reaction is a test for a 1° amine.
steps.why: The reaction needs two hydrogen atoms on the nitrogen, and only a primary amine has them. A secondary amine has one and a tertiary amine has none, so neither can form the isocyanide. That is exactly why the reaction works as a test.
common_mistakes: Saying all amines give the carbylamine reaction. Only primary amines do; 2° and 3° amines give no isocyanide.
Leaving out the conditions. Chloroform and alcoholic KOH with heat must be named for this mark.
steps.memory_tip: Two hydrogens on nitrogen are needed, so only a 1° amine responds. That is why the reaction is a test.
steps.margin_note: The sentence "2° and 3° amines do not respond" is what turns a reaction into a test. Write it.

insider_note: Two marks split cleanly: one for a balanced equation, one for the conditions plus the scope. The line most often left out is that 2° and 3° amines give nothing — without it the answer describes a reaction but not a test.
